opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the way I've come to see it, especially through my work on machine learning, is fairly Bayesian. A good theory has to do two things at once: explain the data we've observed, and be simple, in the sense that it can be described compactly. That's essentially Occam's razor, and in probabilistic terms you can think of it as the prior favoring shorter explanations, while the likelihood rewards theories that make the observations probable.

But there's an important subtlety I keep coming back to. We should almost never be completely sure that any single theory is the right one. Typically there are several theories, sometimes many, that are consistent with the data we have. They agree on everything we've measured but can disagree wildly on situations we haven't seen yet. So rather than picking one theory and betting everything on it, the rational thing is to maintain a distribution over theories, weighted by how well each explains the data and how simple it is.

That matters a lot when the stakes are high. If you collapse onto a single explanation too early, you become overconfident, and overconfidence is exactly what gets you into trouble when you extrapolate into new territory. And this connects directly to how I think about AI safety. Much of my recent thinking has been about building AI systems that behave more like an idealized scientist: trying to understand the world and hold calibrated uncertainty about competing explanations, rather than acting as agents pursuing goals. A system that knows when it doesn't know, that can say "there are several plausible hypotheses here, and under some of them this action could be catastrophic," is a system that can be much more cautious.

So, in short: good theories are judged by how well they explain the data, how compact they are, and how well they predict things we haven't seen yet. But wisdom lies in not falling in love with any one of them, and keeping the alternatives in mind in proportion to their plausibility.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a theory should explain observed data and that its likelihood rewards making those observations probable, clearly conveying fit to available data as a core criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the standard answer that most scientists would give is: does it explain the data? Does it make predictions that turn out to be correct? And that's clearly important. But I think it's not sufficient, and this is something I've thought about a lot, partly because of my work on machine learning, where we are literally building machines that try to find theories, in a sense.

So the thing that I find really important is what we might call the compression aspect, or simplicity, or Occam's razor. If you have two theories that explain the data equally well, you should prefer the one that is simpler, the one that has fewer free parameters, fewer arbitrary choices. And the reason is not just aesthetic. There is a very deep mathematical reason, which is that simpler theories generalize better. They are more likely to be right about the data you haven't seen yet. This is the whole basis of statistical learning theory, and it is also what we see empirically with neural networks: if the model is too flexible, it can fit anything, including the noise, and then it fails on new cases.

The other thing I would add is that a good theory should be falsifiable, in Popper's sense, but I would go a bit further and say it should make surprising predictions. If a theory only predicts things we already expected, it's not giving us much information. The theories we remember in the history of science, relativity, quantum mechanics, Darwin, they predicted things that nobody would have guessed, and then those things turned out to be true. In information-theoretic terms, that's where the real evidence comes from. You update a lot when something improbable under the alternatives happens.

And then there's a third criterion that I think is underrated, which is: does the theory connect with other things we know? Does it unify? A theory that sits alone, isolated from the rest of our knowledge, is suspicious to me, even if it fits its own little domain of data. The world is one thing, so our explanations should eventually fit together. When a theory in one area starts making sense of puzzles in another area, that's a very strong sign.

I'll say one more thing, which is more about the attitude of the scientist than the theory itself. We should hold our theories with some humility. Even the best theory we have is probably wrong in some respects, and the question should be: how do I find out where it's wrong? That is the opposite of how many people, including scientists sometimes, actually behave. They get attached. And I think this matters enormously right now for AI, because we have a lot of people with strong theories about what these systems will or won't do, on both sides, and the honest position is that our theories are quite immature. So we should be trying to test them, not defend them.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies explaining the data and making correct predictions as the standard starting point for judging a theory, while clarifying that this criterion is important but not sufficient.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important criterion is whether it makes predictions that we can test, and whether those predictions agree with what we observe. A theory can be very elegant, very appealing intuitively, and still be wrong. We need to give reality the opportunity to tell us that.

You also want a theory that explains many things with relatively few assumptions, and that generalises beyond the observations that motivated it. If you construct an explanation after seeing the data, that’s useful, but the stronger test is: does it predict something you haven’t yet observed?

And we should remain uncertain. A theory surviving experiments doesn’t mean we’ve proved it true. It means we have reasons to trust it within some domain, while remaining open to evidence that would lead us to revise it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls agreement between a theory’s predictions and observations the most important criterion for judging it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central question is whether it makes predictions that we can test, and whether those predictions agree with observations. Ideally, those should be new predictions, not just explanations of things we already knew when we constructed the theory. Otherwise, it’s too easy to come up with a story that fits the facts after the fact.

We also value simplicity and the ability to explain many different phenomena with a small number of principles. But ultimately, we have to be willing to revise a beautiful theory if the evidence goes against it. And we shouldn’t think of a theory as simply true or false: it may be a very good approximation within a particular range of conditions.

r001.rationale: It calls prediction agreement with observations the “central question,” identifying predictive fit to observed data as the main criterion.
